Moreover, we show that reinforcement learning with credit assignment substantially bolsters the decentralized model, effectively closing the gap with the centralized baseline.

papers.title: JEPA-Tuner: From Predictive Fine-Tuning to Asynchronous Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.

papers.title: Factory-simulator: A process-oriented environment for evaluating manufacturing decisions against optimisation-based references
papers.abstract: Motivated by discussions with an electronics contract manufacturer about decision support, Factory-simulator provides a deterministic manufacturing environment for controlled research on the business performance of large language model-based multi-agent systems (LLM-MAS). Equal delivery performance can arise from decisions with different financial consequences, complicating evaluation through delivery metrics alone. Its process-oriented model connects procurement and production decisions to order fulfilment and factory finances. Seeded worlds and recorded actions support replay and branching from a shared history to examine alternative decisions and their downstream consequences. Linear and mixed-integer programming models generate profit-oriented reference decisions. Observation-limited comparators use disclosed information; full-foresight references use future events for diagnostic comparison. Controlled examples show equal delivery performance with different profit under the same information and distinguish delivery penalties from deferred payment. Verification includes material and financial balances, replay and forks, and a small allocation instance in which the tested optimisation-based controllers attain an analytically established optimum. An external three-role LLM-MAS client completed four illustrative runs comprising 159 periods, with reconciled balances and exact replay of recorded actions. Matched-world rolling comparisons contextualise the financial outcomes, while full-foresight results provide heuristic reference points rather than certified optima. The software enables researchers to investigate how agent organisation and information access affect business outcomes, including whether distributing procurement and production responsibilities changes profit relative to a centralised controller.

papers.title: Population-Based Post-Training for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is one of the most popular post-training paradigms for large language models. RLVR typically trains a single model under hyperparameters chosen before training begins, while researchers tune hyperparameters across consecutive runs. We introduce Population-Based Post-Training (PBPT), which trains several models in parallel and lets the training process do the tuning through population-based training. PBPT periodically evaluates models on a validation set. High-performers are duplicated and their hyperparameters perturbed to explore new configurations. Low-performers stop training and are replaced by these copies. On reasoning benchmarks (Enigmata, Nemotron) and interactive tool-use environments (Gaia2, AppWorld), PBPT produces stronger agents than compute-matched groups of independent RLVR learners. Furthermore, PBPT is able to recover from poor initial hyperparameters, automatically discovering better settings over the course of training.

papers.title: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
papers.abstract: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.

papers.title: LIBERO-MOR: A Multimodal Robustness Benchmark Across the Vision-Language-Action Pipeline
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on robot manipulation benchmarks. Translating this progress into reliable deployment calls for systematic evaluation of how policies respond to variations throughout the robot interaction loop. We introduce LIBERO-MOR, a multimodal robustness benchmark across the vision-language-action pipeline. Built on standard LIBERO, it covers five deployment-facing domains: vision, language, proprioception, action execution, and environment. The benchmark comprises 22 deployment-inspired perturbations, each evaluated at three severity levels across 40 tasks under a paired clean-perturbed protocol, enabling controlled and reproducible comparisons. We evaluate seven representative VLA models spanning diverse action-generation mechanisms. Our experiments reveal substantial robustness gaps behind high clean-task success, together with shared vulnerabilities and distinct model-specific failure patterns across domains. Severity analysis further distinguishes progressive degradation, collapse at stronger interventions, and failures triggered at the mildest tested level. By connecting aggregate performance to pipeline domains, individual perturbations, and intervention strength, LIBERO-MOR provides a systematic framework for diagnosing VLA robustness and guiding the development of more reliable robot policies.

papers.title: EA-Bench: Measuring information and action efficiency under imperfect instructions
papers.abstract: Personal agents help users complete everyday work across digital applications. Many standard benchmarks assume that users provide sufficient information to solve a task. However, agents often encounter incomplete, distracting, or inconsistent information in practice. To systematically study agent inefficiency under such imperfect information, we introduce Efficient Action (EA)-Bench, which evaluates both tool calls and user interactions in work-related tasks. To our knowledge, it is the first benchmark to jointly evaluate tool-call efficiency and user-interaction efficiency under controlled missing, redundant, and conflicting information. We construct 63 base-task instances adapted from existing work-related benchmarks. To guide perturbation design and quantify task requirements, we represent workflows as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and examine node-level dependencies to identify where information can be withheld, contradicted, or supplemented with distractors. We use a two-stage validation process combining AI-assisted checks with expert screening to select 232 conditions from 792 initial candidates. We organize these tasks into Easy and Hard tracks by task complexity. Experiments show that imperfect information can reduce accuracy and increase tool-use and user-interaction costs. More concerning, several models obtain apparently correct outcomes by guessing user-specific values without confirmation, revealing potential execution unreliability in current models under imperfect user information.

papers.title: Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over in both simulation and real-robot settings.

papers.title: DeRail: Escaping Trajectory Priors via Counterfactual Action Steering for Mid-Execution Instruction Switching
papers.abstract: Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the $[15,21]$ switching range, CAS improves $π_{0.5}$ from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. Code will be made publicly available.

papers.title: DiscernBench: Evaluating Cooperative Discernment of LLM Agents in Institutional Settings
papers.abstract: The deployment of large language models in operational settings demands evaluation of judgment under institutional constraint. We introduce DiscernBench, a benchmark for evaluating cooperative discernment: the ability of an agent to determine whether to comply with, refuse, or escalate a request in an institutional setting. DiscernBench comprises scenarios derived from real-world incident reports across domains such as aviation, law enforcement, and emergency management. We evaluate eight LLMs across three decision-making configurations and analyze both final decisions and the intermediate judgments produced during multi-agent deliberation. Under disagreement, Final Responders exhibit model- and role-dependent aggregation patterns in which a lone specialist recommendation can disproportionately influence the collective decision, a phenomenon we term Minority-Signal Override. Role-specialized multi-agent deliberation raises average over-escalation from 3.79% under direct single-agent judgment to 28.27%, with the direction and magnitude of minority-signal influence varying substantially across models and specialist roles. These results reveal distinct collective decision behaviors that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone. Trustworthy multi-agent systems therefore require evaluating not only individual specialist reasoning, but also how conflicting judgments are transformed into collective decisions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Disha1001/DiscernBench.

papers.title: 3DCodeFactory: Scaling Training Data for 3D Code Agents
papers.abstract: As code agents evolve, their scope is expanding from generating simple static 3D meshes to constructing structurally complete, complex, interactive 3D scenes. However, existing datasets mainly rely on converting or captioning pre-existing 3D assets, consisting mostly of single-turn code data for static single objects and struggling to scale task diversity and scene complexity, leaving such training data scarce. We present 3DCodeFactory, an automated framework that directly constructs diverse, complex 3D training data from abundant raw text (e.g., diffusion prompts and product descriptions). The framework first leverages an image generator to synthesize 3D reference images from raw text as visual anchors, guiding the generation of concrete modeling specifications and interactive functional requirements; meanwhile, it jointly constructs visual, specification, and functional rubrics from the reference images and requirements to automatically score and filter multi-turn agent rollouts. Based on this framework, we release 3DCodeFactory-Data, comprising 5,045 high-quality task instances and multi-turn interaction trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B on 3DCodeFactory-Data significantly improves performance on BlenderWorld, P3D-Bench, and 3DCodeBench, consistently outperforming models trained on existing open-source 3D code datasets, with our 27B model further surpassing the same-series 2.4T flagship Qwen3.8-Max in overall performance.

papers.title: Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? An Empirical Study of Hidden AI-Directed Text on GitHub
papers.abstract: AI coding agents now triage issues, review pull requests and pick up tasks inside GitHub repositories, and to do so they read text that anyone with a GitHub account can write. This makes GitHub a prime surface for indirect prompt injection, in which instructions embedded in untrusted content steer a model that later processes it. Prior work has demonstrated such attacks against agents on GitHub in controlled settings, but how often they occur in practice, who deploys them, and for what purpose remain unknown. We present the first large-scale empirical study of AI-directed hidden text on GitHub. We analyzed roughly 145 million issues, pull requests, comments and README files, detected text that GitHub does not render to a human reader but that an agent receives in full, and filtered it with a two-stage LLM classification, a template provenance check and an exhaustive manual review. We identify 2,281 validated findings in issues, pull requests and comments (16 per million items), and AI-directed hidden text in the READMEs of 107 repositories. We find a heterogeneous ecosystem of four uses: attacks on other parties' agents, defensive text that restricts agents, content override that steers what they write, and first-party orchestration, in which projects coordinate their own agents through hidden markers. Attacks are rare (about one in 3.3 million items) but aimed at maintainers' own triage, review and CI agents. Orchestration accounts for two thirds of the findings in issues, pull requests and comments, grew fivefold in four months, and forms a control channel that anyone who can comment can imitate. Replayed offline against five models we tested, the attacks succeed against one small, fast model in 19% of cases, and against none once HTML comments are stripped. We release our detection tool and every finding.

papers.title: VTLA-RL: Learning Visuotactile Policies for Load-Adaptive Grasping
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action foundation models learn general manipulation priors, but object mass and local slip are difficult to infer from vision alone. Changing loads require contact-driven grasp adjustments that demonstrations collected under fixed conditions may not adequately cover. We present VTLA-RL to study visuotactile grasping policies and their reinforcement learning (RL) post-training under varying loads. Our main approach shares a visual encoder between tactile-image histories and RGB inputs to jointly generate and execute motion and bilateral force targets in a unified action space. Mixed real and simulated demonstrations first establish motion and contact priors. Two-stage multi-task RL then uses only simulated interaction to optimize the policy through task-success returns without continued real-demonstration supervision, and the trained policy deploys directly to real robots. We compare tactile representations and RL post-training routes in simulation and separately evaluate load variation and placement perturbations on hardware. The full method achieves higher grasping success than the supervised initialization, while RL post-training gains differ across approaches, providing empirical evidence for choosing representations and training approaches for this task.

papers.title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. This makes a benchmark result conditional on how the workflow is executed. We introduce MASSys, a benchmark for measuring this dependence in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. MASSys executes the same candidate-task pairs across serving substrates and load regimes, using five workload families spanning software repair, research synthesis, financial analysis, interactive control, and diagram generation. It records task quality alongside delivery, latency, cost, resource pressure, and failure evidence. In a controlled motivation diagnostic, the Star workflow falls from first to fourth in mean-latency rank under KV-cache pressure, while Chain rises from fourth to first. The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.

papers.title: RecallWorld: Episodic Memory for Persistent Embodied Video World Models
papers.abstract: Video world models generate plausible novel views but often lack persistent memory, failing to preserve a place's geometry and appearance when an agent revisits a scene. A central challenge is how previous views should be effectively used for creating memory. Reconstructing them independently underutilizes geometric constraints between nearby views, while repeatedly reconstructing a growing history can propagate later prediction errors into earlier geometry. We introduce RecallWorld, a persistent embodied video world model that jointly reconstructs short multi-view episodes into Scenelets while keeping geometry independent across episodes. Starting from a single source image, camera-aware ray lifting places perspective and native fisheye images in a common world frame, retaining wide-field content for perspective generation. Each generated segment extends the Scenelet memory and conditions subsequent generation. Coverage-based retrieval selects complementary Scenelets from the full history, while target-view visibility is resolved geometrically before appearance fusion, providing consistent memory conditioning for guiding subsequent generation. Across four datasets, RecallWorld improves revisit PSNR over the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles, demonstrating substantially stronger preservation of scene identity across exploration and return.

papers.title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

papers.title: Aegis: A Conversational Prototype for Lung Cancer Risk Information and Follow-up
papers.abstract: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. Its documented verification scope comprises 45 functional test specifications covering account management, questionnaire interaction, reporting, doctor-side review, and consultation. The available evaluation describes workflow behavior qualitatively; it provides no per-case execution results, clinical cohort, predictive-performance measurements, or comparative experiments. We therefore present Aegis as an engineering prototype for organizing risk information and follow-up, with clinical validity and the benefits of its agent-based design remaining unestablished. The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.

papers.title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
papers.abstract: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

papers.title: MADRec: Reliable Multi-Agent Reasoning with Evidence-Grounded Debate for Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming recommender systems from conventional preference matching toward reasoning-driven and explainable decision-making. Multi-agent collaboration further advances this paradigm by distributing recommendation reasoning across specialized agents. However, existing frameworks rarely assess the reliability of intermediate reasoning during collaboration, allowing erroneous judgments to propagate across agents and ultimately degrade recommendation quality. To address this issue, we propose Multi-Agent Debate-based Recommendation (MADRec), an evidence-grounded multi-agent framework that enhances the reliability of multi-agent recommendation reasoning. MADRec consists of three coordinated modules. First, the Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) module enables an Interaction Agent and a Semantic Agent to analyze interaction signals and content-level semantic signals from complementary perspectives, generating diverse recommendation judgments through structured debate. Second, the Evidence-Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning (EG-RAR) module grounds the Semantic Agent's reasoning in item-level evidence and refines candidate scores by assessing how well the evidence supports the corresponding semantic claims. Third, the Judge-based Ranking Calibration (JRC) module leverages debate-derived reliability cues to adaptively calibrate interaction-based and semantic ranking results for the final recommendation. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that MADRec consistently outperforms competitive baselines and enhances the reliability of multi-agent recommendation reasoning.
